name: Vera Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy coffee, tea and cafe supplies for Brightwater Food Service, which delivers to about 900 cafes and canteens around Harbourton. My mornings start with a chat to my AI assistant, which pulls overnight price changes and flags which beans are about to run short. Then I'm on video calls with roasters and tea estates, because I love a good origin story and a better margin. The part that wears me out is the weekly spreadsheet war with sales about what they've promised customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, great, a bit more time for the interesting calls. To friends I'd say it's like the dot-com thing, a lot of noise and a few real tools. Online I'd post my favourite prompts anyway, because they work whether the world changes or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel almost disappointed, because I enjoy the tools and was curious where they'd go. My job is safe in this picture, no question. The one thing I'd note is that I already let AI draft my reorder emails, so even the small stuff touches my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes, so I'd keep refining what I do now. I'd build a better automated check on supplier prices, maybe save myself three hours a week. I'd also use that time to start a small newsletter on specialty coffee sourcing, just for fun, and keep 800 a month going into the house fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easy and a little bored. We have the mortgage, but with Jonas's bike shop doing fine and my salary, it's manageable. I'd say it feels like a normal year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even the small stuff touches your day. Which tasks does AI already do for you that you used to do yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drafting supplier emails, comparing quotes in a table, and spotting price jumps before they hit our margins. I used to spend about eight hours a week on that. Now it's maybe three, and I spend the saved time on the phone with growers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what would you do if prices and pay just stayed flat for years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move sideways to category management, because staying in one post for ten years isn't me. Boredom is my main career risk, not AI.

say: I'd tell colleagues it's a bit more time for the **interesting calls**.
To friends I'd say it's like the dot-com bubble, with a few real tools among the noise.
think: I'd feel almost **disappointed**, because I enjoy the tools and was curious where they'd go.
My job is safe here, though AI already drafts my reorder emails.
do: Build a better automated **price check** on supplier quotes, saving about three hours a week.
Start a small **newsletter** on specialty coffee sourcing.
Keep putting **800 a month** into the house fund.
feel: **Easy, a little bored**, like a normal year.
S0.quote: Boredom is my main career risk, not AI.
fieldNote: Vera already uses AI **every day**, so even a plateau means she's ahead of her colleagues.
Treats saved time as room for supplier calls and a newsletter, not as a threat.
Her mood is calm because pay is good, savings are strong and her partner's shop is steady.

steps.text: Build an automated price check on incoming supplier quotes
Start a monthly newsletter on specialty coffee sourcing
Keep putting 800 a month into the house fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, good, let's decide now what we automate and what we keep human, before somebody decides it for us. To friends I'd say, learn the tools, and demand your employer pays for the learning. Online I'd run a thread on which buying tasks go first, with examples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think a third of buying jobs vanish in three years, mine included if I stand still. I'm in the better half because I use it daily, but better half isn't safe. Brightwater has 11 buyers now and I'd be surprised if it's more than 7.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to lead the move of our reorder buying onto an AI agent, because whoever sets it up knows what it does and doesn't do. I'd start offering sourcing advice to a couple of small cafes on weekends, for pay, as a test. And I'd save an extra 400 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fired up and a bit uneasy. It's exciting, honestly, but I'm also one of the people it could shrink. I'd be lying if I said I slept perfectly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said four of the eleven buyers might go. How do you feel about helping set up the thing that replaces them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Conflicted. I'd rather it's me doing it fairly than a consultant doing it without caring. I'd push the company to retrain people for supplier relations and quality, and I'd put that in writing, because I won't help cut colleagues and pretend it's neutral.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the weekend consulting if it worked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it brought in 1,500 a month I'd cut my hours at Brightwater to four days. That gives me a foot in two doors. A small cafe chain wants me full time, and it's a test of whether I could jump.

say: I'd say we should decide now what to **automate** and what to keep human.
Online I'd run a thread with examples of buying tasks that go first.
think: I think a third of buying jobs vanish in **three years**, mine included if I stand still.
Brightwater has 11 buyers and I'd be surprised if it keeps **seven**.
do: Lead the move of reorder buying onto an **AI agent** at Brightwater.
Offer **weekend sourcing advice** to a couple of small cafes for pay.
feel: **Fired up and uneasy**: exciting, but I'm one of the people it could shrink.
S1.quote: I won't help cut colleagues and pretend it's neutral.
fieldNote: Vera tries to **lead** the change rather than wait, and tests a weekend consultancy as a backup.
Strong conscience: she will help automate only if her colleagues get retraining in writing.
Predicts Brightwater's buying team drops from 11 to about 7, and sees herself in the better half.

steps.text: Volunteer to lead moving reorder buying onto an AI agent
Offer paid weekend sourcing advice to two small cafes
Ask management in writing to retrain colleagues for supplier relations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a standing group of buyers, sales and management to plan this week by week, and I'd volunteer. To friends I'd say, get your savings tidy and learn the tools yesterday. Online I'd push hard for a government plan, because companies alone won't move at that speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job as it exists is gone by 2028, but I'd be reachable for the next job because I'm used to the tools. What scares me is everyone else I know. Jonas's shop is hands-on, so he gets till 2031, but the customers who buy bikes from him might lose their jobs first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Month one, I'd freeze spending on anything we don't need and push my side consulting hard, aiming at the small cafes who want help and can't afford a full-time buyer. I'd also ask Brightwater for a role designing the AI buying system. And I'd write to my representative about a basic income pilot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a lot of adrenaline. It's a sprint, and I'm good at sprints. But there's a hard edge to it, because two years is also when Noor starts secondary school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned customers losing jobs first. How would that hit Jonas's bike shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer people buying 2,000 bikes and repairs when they're worried about their jobs. He'd see a drop of maybe 30 percent within a year. Our household would rely on my pay and savings, so I'd want to keep earning as long as possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughters Noor and Elsa that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughters Noor and Elsa that robots and computers are going to be everywhere and we'll learn it together. I'd say we're lucky, we have savings, and some families won't be. I'd make them help me pack cupboards for the food bank on Saturday, to make it real.

say: I'd say we need a standing group of buyers, sales and management to plan **week by week**.
Online I'd push for a **government plan**, since companies alone won't move this fast.
think: My job as it exists is **gone by 2028**, but my daily AI use keeps me reachable.
Jonas's bike shop could lose **30 percent** of sales as customers fear for their jobs.
do: Freeze all non-essential spending and push **weekend consulting** to small cafes.
Ask Brightwater for a role **designing** the AI buying system.
Write to my representative about a **basic income pilot**.
feel: **Anxious, with adrenaline**: it's a sprint, and I'm good at sprints.
S2.quote: I'd tell my daughters Noor and Elsa that robots and computers are going to be everywhere and we'll learn it together.
fieldNote: Vera responds to danger with **speed**: freeze spending, push consulting, ask for a design role.
Worries about her partner's bike shop, whose customers lose work first even though his trade is hands-on.
Wants her daughters involved in practical solidarity, such as helping fill cupboards for the food bank.

steps.text: Freeze spending on anything the household doesn't need
Sign up small cafes for paid weekend sourcing advice
Ask Brightwater for a role designing the AI buying system
Write to my representative about a basic income pilot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is long enough that you can't hide behind it. To friends I'd say, start learning something that combines people and AI. Online I'd write about the buyers who'll lead teams of agents and the ones who'll be replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel energised and slightly guilty about it. With five years I could build a second income from consulting, and get the house nearly paid off. The guilt is that other people, in warehouses and cafes, don't have the same toolkit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to grow the sourcing consultancy to a few paying cafes and the newsletter to 2,000 subscribers. I'd take a short course on supply contracts and negotiation theory. And I'd put 1,000 a month toward the mortgage, so the house is almost ours by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but upbeat. Five years gives me room to be clever. I'd say I'd be one of the people who wins, but I'd feel better if I could bring others with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel guilty. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer my newsletter readers and the Brightwater warehouse team a free monthly session on using AI for ordering and stock counts. I can't save everybody, but I can pass on what I know. I'd also back the union's call for retraining money from the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between this and the 2028 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the 2028 picture I'd be sprinting to stay in work, but here I'd be building something I own. That is a different feeling, closer to excitement than fear.

say: I'd say five years is long enough that **nobody** can hide behind it.
Online I'd write about buyers who'll **lead teams of agents** and those replaced by them.
think: I'd feel **energised** and slightly guilty, because others lack my toolkit.
I could build a second income and nearly pay off the **house**.
do: Grow the sourcing consultancy to several **paying cafes** and the newsletter to 2,000 readers.
Take a short course on **supply contracts** and negotiation.
Put **1,000 a month** toward the mortgage.
feel: **Uneasy but upbeat**: five years gives me room to be clever.
S3.quote: In the 2028 picture I'd be sprinting to stay in work, but here I'd be building something I own.
fieldNote: Extra time turns her from sprinting to **building**: consultancy, newsletter, mortgage.
Feels some guilt about colleagues without her tools and plans free monthly sessions.
Backs the union's call for company-paid retraining despite her own comfortable position.

steps.text: Grow the sourcing consultancy to several paying cafes
Take a short course on supply contracts and negotiation
Put 1,000 a month toward the mortgage
Run a free monthly session on AI ordering for warehouse staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so let's build a proper reskilling programme instead of one-off courses. To friends I'd say, play with the tools every day and keep a hobby that isn't screens. Online I'd keep posting prompts and ideas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel calm about me and slightly protective about the kids. Elsa and Noor would be 19 and 22 in 2036, right in the middle of it. I'd want them to learn how to work with the tools and to have a trade they're proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep trading up, probably into a senior category role or a sourcing consultancy of my own by 2031. I'd keep saving, since the mortgage would be gone by then. And I'd put money into the girls' studies and a bit into shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, excited even. A decade is a long runway, and I like long runways. I might even enjoy the ride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want the girls to have a trade they're proud of. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my daughters Elsa and Noor to have something where they can see what they made, like food, design or repair. I've seen friends who work in pure screens burn out. I'd also want them to be comfortable talking to machines and to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest thing you'd do in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take part of my salary and put it into a fund for the girls, 500 a month, and open a small share account for myself. If the money is working while I'm learning, I sleep better.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so build a proper **reskilling programme** instead of one-off courses.
To friends I'd say, play with the tools daily and keep a **non-screen hobby**.
think: I'd feel **calm** about myself and a little protective of the kids.
Elsa and Noor would be 19 and 22 in 2036, right in the middle of it.
do: Trade up to a **senior category role** or my own sourcing consultancy by 2031.
Put **500 a month** into a fund for the girls' studies.
Open a small **share account** for myself.
feel: **Calm, even excited**: a decade is a long runway and I like long runways.
S4.quote: I'd want my daughters Elsa and Noor to have something where they can see what they made, like food, design or repair.
fieldNote: Her calm rests on **adaptability** and a strong cushion, not on any belief that AI is overhyped.
Protective about her daughters' futures and steers them towards visible, hands-on work.
Plans to invest 500 a month for the girls and open a small share account.

steps.text: Move up into a senior category role or start my own consultancy
Put 500 a month into a fund for the girls' studies
Open a small share account and add to it monthly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, for sure, because even with all my habits I'd be sprinting and the people around me wouldn't have a head start. What would help is a plan from government and employers: paid retraining, income support while people switch, and honest dates. I don't want to be the lone winner in a street of losers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Adaptable doesn't mean unaffected. I use these tools every day, and I still lie awake wondering what my daughters will do for work. I may be quick, but I don't know the answers.

headlineQuote: Adaptable doesn't mean unaffected. I use these tools every day, and I still lie awake wondering what my daughters will do for work.
portrait: Vera is a **43-year-old buyer** of coffee and tea for a food-service distributor, and she uses AI tools every day.
She leans left and backs **unions**, public plans and retraining, while moving first on her own career.
She runs a sourcing **newsletter** and tests weekend consulting as a second income.
Her mood only reaches anxious in the 2028 picture, thanks to speed, savings and a head start.
Her worry is wider than herself: colleagues without her tools, her partner's customers and her **two daughters**.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, because even her head start can't carry others in time.
whatWouldHelp: A plan from government and employers: **paid retraining**, income support and honest dates.
